topic.title: SQL & Databases
topic.description: Query, join, filter, aggregate. The universal language of data.

items.prompt: What does SQL stand for?
What is a RELATIONAL DATABASE?
options: A database for storing relationships only
A database with a single table
A database that organizes data into tables (rows and columns) with defined relationships between them

items.prompt: Which is a TRUE statement about SQL?
options: It is mostly standardized across database engines, with small dialect differences (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server)
SQL only works in one specific database
Each database uses a completely different language
SQL is being replaced by NoSQL

items.prompt: Which is a popular OPEN-SOURCE relational database?
Why is SQL still HIGHLY relevant in 2026?
options: It only works on old systems
Most business data still lives in relational databases — every data engineer/analyst/backend dev needs it

items.prompt: What is a TABLE in SQL?
options: A collection of related data organized into rows and columns with a defined schema

items.prompt: What is a ROW (record) in a table?
options: A single entry containing one value for each column

items.prompt: What is a COLUMN (field) in a table?
options: A named attribute with a specific data type that every row in the table can have a value for

items.prompt: What is a SCHEMA in SQL?
options: The structure (tables, columns, types, constraints) that defines how data is organized

items.prompt: What is a NULL value?
options: A special marker meaning 'no value' or 'unknown' — distinct from 0 or empty string

items.prompt: Which query retrieves all columns from the users table?
How do you select SPECIFIC columns?
options: SELECT name AND email IN users;

items.prompt: How do you LIMIT the number of returned rows?
options: SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 10;  (or TOP 10 in SQL Server)

items.prompt: How do you RENAME a column in the query output?
options: SELECT name AS user_name FROM users;

items.prompt: What does `SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products;` do?
options: Returns only the most popular category

items.prompt: How do you FILTER rows?
Which operator checks if a value is IN a list?
options: WHERE status BETWEEN active AND pending

items.prompt: What does `WHERE name LIKE 'A%'` do?
options: Matches names with at least one A
Matches rows where name is exactly 'A%'
Matches rows where name starts with 'A' (% is the wildcard for any sequence)

items.prompt: How do you check for a NULL value?
How do you combine multiple conditions?
How do you SORT results?
options: SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY age;
SELECT * FROM users WITH age ORDER;
SELECT * FROM users SORT BY age;

items.prompt: How do you sort by MULTIPLE columns?
Where do NULL values appear in an ORDER BY?
options: Database-dependent — PostgreSQL puts them last by default; you can control with NULLS FIRST/LAST

items.prompt: What does `ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 10` give you?
How do you PAGINATE results (page 2 of 10 per page)?
Which aggregation COUNTS rows?
options: COUNT(*) — counts all rows; COUNT(column) — counts non-NULL values

items.prompt: Which aggregation SUMS values?
What does AVG return for an empty result?
What does GROUP BY do?
options: Groups rows sharing a value, so aggregations are computed per group

items.prompt: What's the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
options: WHERE filters individual rows BEFORE grouping; HAVING filters groups AFTER grouping

items.prompt: What is a JOIN in SQL?
options: A clause that combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column

items.prompt: What does an INNER JOIN return?
options: All rows from the right table only
All rows from the left table only
Only rows that have matches in BOTH tables based on the join condition

items.prompt: What does a LEFT JOIN do?
options: Returns ALL rows from the left table, plus matching right-table rows (NULL if no match)

items.prompt: Which join clause specifies HOW tables relate?
What is a FOREIGN KEY?
options: A column referencing the primary key of another table — enforces referential integrity

items.prompt: How do you INSERT a new row?
How do you INSERT multiple rows at once?
How do you UPDATE rows?
options: UPDATE users SET email = 'new@x.com' WHERE id = 5;

items.prompt: What's the BIG RISK with `DELETE FROM users;`?
options: It backs up the data first automatically
Without a WHERE clause, this deletes EVERY row in the table

items.prompt: What's the DIFFERENCE between DELETE and TRUNCATE?
options: DELETE removes rows (one by one, with WHERE); TRUNCATE empties the entire table fast but resets sequences
DELETE is for tables, TRUNCATE for databases

items.prompt: What is a PRIMARY KEY?
options: A column (or set of columns) that uniquely identifies each row in a table

items.prompt: Why use a UNIQUE constraint?
options: Ensures no two rows have the same value for that column (e.g., email)

items.prompt: What is an INDEX in SQL?
options: A data structure that speeds up queries by enabling fast lookups (like a book's index)

items.prompt: When does an index NOT help a query?
options: All of the above are partially true
When the WHERE clause uses a function on the column (e.g., WHERE LOWER(email) = ...)

items.prompt: What's the DOWNSIDE of too many indexes?
options: Each index slows down INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and takes extra disk space

items.prompt: Which is a COMMON SQL data type?
options: INTEGER, VARCHAR/TEXT, BOOLEAN, DATE, TIMESTAMP, DECIMAL

items.prompt: What does NOT NULL do?
options: Constrains a column so it cannot have NULL values — every row MUST have a value

items.prompt: What does DEFAULT do?
options: Sets a value to use when none is provided on INSERT (e.g., DEFAULT NOW() for timestamps)

items.prompt: What's the difference between VARCHAR(n) and TEXT?
options: VARCHAR has a length limit; TEXT can hold unlimited (or very large) text — depends on the database engine

items.prompt: What does CHECK do?
options: Verifies the entire table for errors
Constrains a column to only allow values matching a condition (e.g., CHECK (age >= 0))

items.prompt: What is a SUBQUERY?
options: A query nested inside another query — its result is used by the outer query

items.prompt: What is a CTE (Common Table Expression)?
options: A named temporary result set defined with WITH, usable in the main query — more readable than nested subqueries

items.prompt: When should you PREFER a CTE over a subquery?
options: For complex queries, repeated subexpressions, or when readability matters

items.prompt: What is a RECURSIVE CTE used for?
options: Querying hierarchical/tree data — e.g., organizational charts, comment trees, category trees

items.prompt: What does EXISTS check?
options: Whether a column exists in the table
Whether a subquery returns ANY rows — efficient for 'does X exist?' checks

items.prompt: What is a WINDOW FUNCTION?
options: A function that opens a window
A function that computes across a set of rows (a 'window') without collapsing them like GROUP BY

items.prompt: What does ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ...) do?
options: Assigns a sequential number to each row based on the ordering

items.prompt: What does PARTITION BY do in a window function?
options: Computes the window function SEPARATELY within each group, but doesn't collapse rows

items.prompt: What does RANK() do?
options: Assigns ranks with ties getting the same rank, leaving gaps (1, 2, 2, 4)

items.prompt: What does LAG() do?
options: Returns a value from a PREVIOUS row — great for comparing each row to the row before it

items.prompt: What is a TRANSACTION?
options: A group of SQL statements treated as one unit — all succeed or all fail together (atomicity)

items.prompt: What does ACID stand for in databases?
How do you start a transaction?
When does data become PERMANENT in a transaction?
options: After COMMIT — until then changes are visible only to your transaction

items.prompt: What is a 'race condition' in databases?
options: When queries run faster than expected
When concurrent transactions interact unexpectedly, leading to incorrect results

items.prompt: What is database NORMALIZATION?
options: Making all tables the same size
Organizing data to reduce redundancy and improve integrity (typically through forms 1NF, 2NF, 3NF)

items.prompt: What's a ONE-TO-MANY relationship?
options: One row maps to one row
One row in table A relates to many rows in table B (e.g., one user has many orders)

items.prompt: What's a MANY-TO-MANY relationship?
options: Both sides relate to multiple of each other — implemented with a JUNCTION TABLE in between

items.prompt: When is DENORMALIZATION appropriate?
options: When read performance is critical and the cost of duplicated data is acceptable (often in analytics/reporting tables)

items.prompt: What's a JUNCTION TABLE?
options: The first table in the database
A table connecting two others to model many-to-many relationships (also called bridge/link/join table)

items.prompt: What does EXPLAIN do?
options: Runs the query in slow motion
Shows how the database PLANS to execute your query — essential for performance tuning

items.prompt: Why is `SELECT *` discouraged in production?
options: Returns more data than needed, harms performance, and breaks if schema changes

items.prompt: What's a SLOW QUERY?
options: A query taking too long — usually because it scans large tables without using indexes

items.prompt: What's a COMMON cause of slow JOINs?
options: Missing index on the foreign key / join column

items.prompt: What is 'N+1 queries'?
options: An anti-pattern where code runs 1 query then N additional queries (often hidden in ORMs)

items.prompt: What is NoSQL?
options: Non-relational databases (document, key-value, graph, column-family) designed for different access patterns
A NoSQL stands for No Standard Query Language

items.prompt: Which is a popular DOCUMENT database?
Which is a popular KEY-VALUE store?
options: Redis (in-memory, blazing fast — used for caching, sessions, queues)

items.prompt: When might NoSQL be a BETTER choice than SQL?
options: Massive horizontal scaling, very flexible schema, or specific access patterns (graphs, time-series)

items.prompt: What does CAP theorem say?
options: A distributed system can guarantee only 2 of: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance

items.prompt: What is SQL INJECTION?
options: An attack where user input is treated as SQL code, letting attackers run arbitrary queries

items.prompt: How do you PREVENT SQL injection?
options: Use parameterized queries / prepared statements — NEVER concatenate user input into SQL strings

items.prompt: Why shouldn't you store passwords as PLAIN TEXT in a database?
options: If the database is breached, all passwords are exposed — use a strong hash like bcrypt or Argon2 instead

items.prompt: What is the PRINCIPLE OF LEAST PRIVILEGE for databases?
options: Use the root user for everything
Give each app/user only the minimum DB permissions they need (no DROP TABLE for a read-only API)

items.prompt: What's a SAFE way to manage database credentials?
options: Environment variables or a secrets manager — NEVER commit them to git
Store them in a public README
Hardcode them in the source code

items.prompt: What is a SERVERLESS database?
options: A managed database that automatically scales without provisioning servers (e.g., Neon, PlanetScale, Supabase)
A database that runs in the browser
A database with no server at all

items.prompt: What is an ORM?
options: Object-Relational Mapper — translates between database tables and code objects (Prisma, SQLAlchemy, Django ORM)

items.prompt: What is a 'migration' in databases?
options: A version-controlled change to the database schema, applied in order across environments

items.prompt: What's a vector database used for?
options: Storing and searching high-dimensional vectors (embeddings) for AI similarity search

items.prompt: What is SQLite often used for?
options: Embedded local databases — every smartphone, browser, and many apps ship with it

items.prompt: What's a GOOD column naming convention?
options: snake_case lowercase: created_at, user_id (consistent, portable, readable)

items.prompt: Which is a HEALTHY rule about database backups?
options: Manual once a year is enough
Automate them, test the restore process regularly, and keep multiple recent + older copies
Store backups on the same server

items.prompt: Why is keeping production data OUT of dev environments important?
options: Privacy (real user data in dev exposes them to breaches and developer access), compliance, and reduces blast radius

items.prompt: Which is a SMART approach to writing complex SQL?
options: Write everything as a giant subquery
Use CTEs, format with indentation, comment intent, and test incrementally with small datasets first

items.prompt: What's the GOLDEN RULE for destructive operations?
options: Just run it and see what happens
Always test with SELECT first, run in a transaction, and have a backup before UPDATE/DELETE on large datasets

items.prompt: What's the BEST way to learn SQL deeply?
options: Work with real data — connect to a database, run real queries, optimize slow ones

items.prompt: Which SQL skill makes you most VALUABLE in the job market?
options: Comfortable with JOINs, window functions, CTEs, and reading EXPLAIN output

items.prompt: How can AI help you LEARN SQL?
options: Explain queries you don't understand, suggest optimizations, generate sample data — but always verify the SQL it writes
Have AI run your production queries

items.prompt: Which is a STRONG project to practice SQL?
options: Pick a public dataset (Kaggle, government open data), import it, and answer real questions about it

items.prompt: What's the MOST important meta-skill in working with databases?
options: Caring deeply about data integrity, performance, and security — small mistakes have big consequences at scale
